newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - PepsiCo CFO sees international focus.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - PepsiCo CFO sees international focus.

text.p: Once PepsiCo Inc completes the $11 billion spin-off of its restaurant operations, it will focus on improving its international beverage business, the company's chief financial officer said on Thursday.

"The international beverage business is least healthy," Karl von der Heyden, who is also PepsiCo's vice chairman, said in a late-afternoon telephone interview with Reuters. "We're going to spend a lot of time and effort and focus working on that."

He made his comments after PepsiCo said it would spin off its restaurant operations -- Kentucky Fried Chicken, Pizza Hut and Taco Bell -- which have about 30,000 locations around the world. In 1995, they accounted for 37 percent of the company's $30.42 billion in revenue and 24 percent of profits, which were $1.6 billion, or $1.00 per share.
PepsiCo in the fourth quarter will distribute shares of its restaurant operations to existing shareholders rather than sell the operations as an initial public offering, von der Heyden said.
He said the company had not yet determined how many shares of the restaurant company it would distribute or fix financial terms. The company said it would not take a charge for the spin-off.
A PepsiCo spokesman said the company did not yet know when the new company's shares would trade on the stock market.
After the spin-off, PepsiCo will be left with its snack foods and beverage operations and would hold all of PepsiCo's current debt of about $9 billion, the company said.
According to von der Heyden, the debt is not too much of a burden because the snack foods and beverage operations are "high margin businesses with predictable cash flows."
"Some of the cash we get from the spin-off will also be used to pay down the debt," he said.

He also said the spin-off will sharpen PepsiCo's focus on international beverages, an area plagued by troubles. Last year, the company reported big operating losses at its Argentina and Brazil bottlers. The loss of its Venezuela bottler to archrival Coca Cola Co was an embarrassing setback.

Partly as a result, PepsiCo in September said it would restructure its international beverage operations and take a total of $525 million in charges. At the time, the company said it aimed to trim its international beverage businesses' operating expenses by about $100 million a year through the restructuring.

"(The strategy) for our international beverages is to go back to the basics," von der Heyden said after the spin-off announcement. "We need to define our primary markets and be very focused ... We also need to make sure our infrastructures are correct and that we're spending accordingly on vending machines and other items."
He declined to be more specific, saying that doing so would yield important information to Coca Cola.

PepsiCo on Thursday also said it would examine the possibility of selling its PepsiCo Food Systems unit, which distributes more than $3 billion worth of restaurant equipment and supplies each year, mostly to PepsiCo's restaurants.

The company's plan regarding PFS -- as it is commonly known -- is to sell it in a private sale, von der Heyden said. He added that PepsiCo has already hired Merrill Lynch & Co to help it find a buyer for the unit, although declined to specify a value for any potential transaction.
Before the announcement, PepsiCo's stock rose 2-3/8 to close at 34-1/4 amid speculation about of a spin-off.
Terry Bivens, an analyst at Donald & Co, said the shares could rise to as high as $42 per share in the new few weeks as investors weigh PepsiCo's plan.
